questions.question: Which expression gives the same table as `df.pivot_table(index="cabin_class", columns="sex", values="fare")`?
options: `df.groupby("cabin_class")["fare"].mean()`, because the default pivot aggregate groups by the row key only and ignores the columns key.
`df.groupby(["cabin_class", "sex"])["fare"].sum()`, because pivoting adds up the values in each cell.
`df.sort_values(["cabin_class", "sex"])["fare"]`, because a pivot is a two-key sort of the column.
`df.groupby(["cabin_class", "sex"])["fare"].mean().unstack()`, because a pivot is a two-key group followed by an unstack.
questions.explanation: A pivot table is a two-key groupby whose second key is moved into the columns with `unstack`, and the default aggregate is the mean. A one-key groupby has no columns key, a sum is a different aggregate, and sorting aggregates nothing.
questions.misconception: The default `aggfunc` of `pivot_table` is the mean, not the sum.

questions.question: What does `margins=True` add to a pivot table?
options: An `All` row and column with the overall aggregate for each row, column, and the whole table.
A blank border of missing values around the whole table, added purely to make it easier to read.
A column showing the standard deviation of every row in the table.
A second copy of the table sorted in descending order of the cell values.
questions.explanation: Margins add subtotals computed with the same `aggfunc`, labelled `All`, along both axes. They do not add padding, a spread column, or a sorted copy.
questions.misconception: The `All` cells are aggregates of the underlying rows, not averages of the displayed cells.

questions.scenario: A pivot of expense totals by weekday and income-or-expense shows `NaN` in cells where no entries exist, and you want the chart to treat those as zero.
questions.question: What should you pass?
options: `dropna=True`, because it removes the weekdays that have no entries from the finished chart entirely.
`margins=True`, because the `All` row replaces any empty cell with a total.
`fill_value=0`, because it replaces empty cells with zero in the finished table.
`aggfunc="count"`, because a count of nothing is always zero.
questions.explanation: `fill_value` fills the cells that have no data after aggregation. `dropna` removes whole columns of missing results rather than filling them, margins add totals, and changing the aggregate changes the meaning of every cell.
questions.misconception: Empty combinations produce `NaN` unless you fill them.

questions.question: How do you get the mean fare and the total survivors in one pivot table?
options: Pass `aggfunc=["mean", "sum"]` without any `values` argument, and pandas matches the functions to the columns.
Run two pivot tables and add them together, because one call can use only one aggregate.
Pass `aggfunc={"fare": "mean", "survived": "sum"}`, a dictionary of column to function.
Pass `values=["fare", "survived"]` and `aggfunc="mean"`, which averages both columns together.
questions.explanation: A dictionary assigns each value column its own aggregate. A list applies every function to every column, and a single aggregate treats both columns the same way.
questions.misconception: `aggfunc` can be a dictionary, not only one function.

questions.question: A column has a missing name. What happens with `names.str.upper()` compared with `[n.upper() for n in names]`?
options: Both raise an `AttributeError` on the missing value, because `None` has no `upper`.
Both skip the missing value and return a shorter list, so the result has no gap where it used to be.
The `.str` version returns `NaN` for the missing value, while the list comprehension raises an `AttributeError`.
The `.str` version raises an error, while the list comprehension fills the gap with an empty string.
questions.explanation: The `.str` accessor propagates missing values, so the column keeps its length with a gap. A plain comprehension calls `upper` on `None` and fails.
questions.misconception: Vectorized string methods are missing-value safe.

questions.scenario: Each name looks like `Mallory, Mr. Lionel` and you want the text after the first comma, split once at the first full stop, in two separate columns.
questions.question: Which approach fits?
options: `s.str.split(".", n=1, expand=True)`, which splits at the first full stop only and returns two columns.
`s.str.split(".")`, which returns two separate columns automatically because there is a single full stop in each name.
`s.str.get(1)`, which returns the second piece of every name without needing a split.
`s.str.replace(".", " ")`, which separates the title into a new column of its own and leaves the rest alone.
questions.explanation: `n=1` limits the number of splits and `expand=True` turns the pieces into columns. Without `expand` the result is a Series of lists, and `get` needs lists to index into.

questions.question: Why does the note pass `regex=False` to `str.replace` when swapping `"Capt"` for `"Officer"`?
options: Because regular expressions cannot match capital letters at all, so plain text matching is the only possible choice.
Because plain text should be matched literally; a character such as `.` would otherwise be read as a pattern.
Because `regex=False` makes the replacement case-insensitive for every title in the column, whatever its capitalization.
Because `str.replace` raises an error unless the argument is set explicitly in every call.
questions.explanation: The default for pattern matching changed between pandas versions, so being explicit avoids surprises. With `regex=False` characters like `.` are literal. It has nothing to do with case, and the call works without it.
questions.misconception: Special characters in a replacement string can be read as regex.

questions.question: What does `names.str.contains("lionel", case=False)` return?
options: A boolean Series that is `True` where the name contains the text, ignoring letter case.
A Series of the names that contain the text, with all other names removed.
The position of the text inside each name as a number, or -1 where the text is missing from a name.
A single `True` or `False` that says whether any one name in the whole column contains the text.
questions.explanation: `contains` returns one boolean per element. To keep the matching rows, use that mask inside square brackets. Positions come from `find`, and `any()` would give a single result.
questions.misconception: `contains` returns a mask, not the filtered rows.

questions.scenario: You need family names that start and end with a consonant. A colleague uses `contains("[^aeiou]")` and gets almost every name.
questions.question: Why, and what pattern fixes it?
options: The pattern is case sensitive, so adding `case=False` is the only fix that is needed to restrict it to the edges.
`contains` cannot use character classes at all, so the check has to be written as an explicit Python loop.
The pattern matches any consonant anywhere; anchors give `^[^aeiou].*[^aeiou]$` to test only the first and last characters.
The pattern needs `str.extract` instead, because `contains` returns the wrong type whenever a class is used.
questions.explanation: Without anchors, a name matches if it contains any consonant anywhere. `^` pins the start and `$` pins the end, so the pattern tests only the edges. Case sensitivity is a separate concern.
questions.misconception: Unanchored patterns match anywhere in the string.

questions.question: Which statement about the date types is correct?
options: Python `datetime` is the fastest of the three types, so pandas uses it internally for large arrays of dates.
NumPy `datetime64` stores dates as 64-bit integers, and the pandas `Timestamp` builds on it with richer methods.
The pandas `Timestamp` has day precision only, so times of day always need a separate type of their own.
All three types are interchangeable and differ only in what they are called.
questions.explanation: NumPy's `datetime64` gives vectorized storage and arithmetic. `Timestamp` combines that with the convenience of `datetime` and has nanosecond precision. Python `datetime` objects are slow at scale.
questions.misconception: Pandas dates are NumPy-backed, not Python-object-backed.

questions.question: How do `pd.date_range("2024-03-01", "2024-03-12", freq="B")` and `freq="D"` differ?
options: `"B"` gives business days, skipping Saturdays and Sundays, while `"D"` gives every calendar day.
`"B"` gives every second day, while `"D"` gives every day, starting from the first date.
`"B"` gives dates in backward order from the end date, while `"D"` gives dates in forward order.
They give the same dates, because the frequency only changes how the index prints.
questions.explanation: `"B"` is business-day frequency, so weekends are skipped. `"D"` is the calendar-day default. The frequency changes which dates exist, not just how they print.
questions.misconception: Frequency codes choose which dates are generated.

questions.scenario: A text column of dates contains a few entries such as "not a date", and `pd.to_datetime` stops with an error.
questions.question: What is the safest way to convert it and keep going?
options: Delete the column and re-enter all of the dates by hand, since pandas cannot read a column of mixed text.
Use `pd.to_datetime(col, errors="coerce")`, which turns unreadable entries into `NaT` so you can inspect them.
Use `astype(int)` first, because a number is always readable as a date.
Call `fillna(0)` on the text column, because zeros are valid dates.
questions.explanation: `errors="coerce"` replaces unparseable values with `NaT`, the missing marker for dates, so conversion completes and the bad rows are easy to find. Integers and zeros are not parsed as dates in the same way.
questions.misconception: Bad values can be turned into missing markers instead of stopping the run.

questions.question: Once a column holds real datetimes, how do you get the weekday name of every row?
options: `col.str.day_name()`, because weekday names are text and so belong to the `.str` accessor.
`col.day_name`, because the weekday is an attribute of the whole column.
`col.dt.day_name()`, because the `.dt` accessor exposes the parts of datetimes.
`col.apply(day_name)`, because pandas provides a global function with that name for every column.
questions.explanation: `.dt` is the datetime accessor, parallel to `.str` for text. It offers `year`, `month_name()`, `day_name()`, `is_month_end`, and more. The `.str` accessor works only on strings.

questions.question: Why is `pd.to_datetime(col, format="%m/%d/%Y %H:%M")` better than leaving the format out for a ledger with dates like `3/2/2022 10:11`?
options: It states whether `3/2` means March 2 or 2 March, avoiding guesses, and parses faster.
It converts the column to plain strings, which makes the later extraction of date parts easier.
It silently drops rows that do not match the pattern, which cleans the ledger.
It is required, because pandas cannot read any slash-separated date without it.
questions.explanation: A date such as 3/2/2022 is ambiguous between month-first and day-first layouts. Giving the format removes the ambiguity and lets the parser skip format inference. Without a format, pandas can still read it, and unmatched rows raise errors rather than being dropped.
questions.misconception: Ambiguous date text should have an explicit format.

questions.question: Explain what the `.str` and `.dt` accessors are for, and what they have in common.
questions.answer: `.str` exposes vectorized text methods such as `lower`, `split`, `contains`, and `replace`, and `.dt` exposes the parts and calendar properties of datetime values such as `year`, `month_name`, and `is_month_end`. Both work on a whole column at once and propagate missing values, so no Python loop is needed.
questions.explanation: Both accessors only work on a column that already has the matching dtype.
